nameStory: The Threespine Stickleback gets its name from the three sharp spines that stand like tiny soldiers along its back, just in front of the dorsal fin. These needle-like spines can lock upright when the fish feels threatened, making it a prickly mouthful for predators. The 'stickleback' part comes from these distinctive back spines that early anglers would feel poking through their nets.
description: The Threespine Stickleback is a small, torpedo-shaped fish that rarely grows longer than your finger - typically 2-4 inches. Its most striking feature is the row of three sharp spines along its back, which can pop up like a switchblade when danger approaches. During breeding season, males develop brilliant colors with bright red bellies and blue-green backs, while females and non-breeding fish appear more silvery-brown with darker vertical bars along their sides.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Streamlined, torpedo-shaped body that feels firm and muscular when gently handled, with a narrow tail base that tapers dramatically from the deeper mid-body

idTips.label: Spines
idTips.description: Three prominent, sharp spines along the back that you can feel even through a net - they lock upright when the fish is stressed and lie flat when relaxed

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Small, fan-shaped dorsal fin behind the spines, and notably reduced pelvic fins that appear as small spines with tiny fin membranes beneath the belly

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Breeding males flash brilliant red bellies and metallic blue-green backs, while females and juveniles show muted brown-silver with dark vertical bars

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Consistently small - adults rarely exceed 4 inches and feel surprisingly light and delicate when netted

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in shallow, weedy areas of both fresh and salt water, often seen in small schools darting between aquatic plants

habitat: Threespine Sticklebacks thrive in shallow, vegetated waters throughout New England, from freshwater ponds and slow streams to salt marshes and coastal tidepools. They prefer areas with plenty of aquatic plants like pondweed or eelgrass where they can dart between stems for cover. You'll often spot them in the shallows of marshes, quiet lake edges, and even brackish areas where rivers meet the sea.

seasonality.spring: Males develop their spectacular breeding colors in late spring, with fiery red bellies that are unmistakable. This is prime time to observe their famous nest-building behavior in shallow water.
seasonality.summer: Peak breeding season when territorial males guard their round, woven nests and can be quite bold, sometimes approaching within inches of observers. Look for courtship displays and schools of juveniles in weedy shallows.
seasonality.fall: Breeding colors fade as fish form loose schools in deeper water. Young-of-the-year appear as tiny silver fish with clearly visible spine outlines.
seasonality.winter: Fish remain active under ice in shallow areas, appearing uniformly brown-silver. Schools may concentrate in slightly deeper sections of their habitat.

funFact: Male Threespine Sticklebacks are among the most devoted fathers in the fish world - they build elaborate round nests from aquatic plants glued together with kidney secretions, then fan the eggs with their fins for over a week to keep them oxygenated, barely leaving to eat during this time!
confusionNotes: The only other stickleback in New England waters is the Blackspotted Stickleback, but it's quite rare and has distinctive black spots scattered across its body. Remember: if you can count exactly three spines on the back and there are no obvious black spots, you've got a Threespine Stickleback.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their small size, Threespine Sticklebacks are considered one of the most important fish in biological research, having contributed to our understanding of evolution, behavior, and ecology more than almost any other species. They're living in both your local pond and the pages of countless scientific journals!
compareHints: The Blackspotted Stickleback, its closest New England relative, is much rarer and distinguished by scattered black spots across its body and sides. Blackspotteds also tend to stay in saltwater environments, while Threespines freely move between fresh and salt water. If you're seeing sticklebacks in freshwater ponds or streams, they're almost certainly the three-spined variety.

relatedSpecies.distinction: While both blackspotted and threespine sticklebacks share the characteristic three back spines and similar body shape, the blackspotted variety is distinguished by its scattered dark spots and preference for staying in saltier coastal waters rather than venturing into freshwater streams.
